Dear unmarked users,

I`m using the colext function to understand the impact of hurricane Maria on birds and frogs distribution in Puerto Rico. 

I`m working with 68 sampling sites in three transects along an elevational gradient (~75-1030meters), three primary visits (years), and 17 secondary occasions.

One of my main questions in this study is to determine if species changed their distributions along the elevational gradient among the years (especially in the year after the hurricane).

As I understand, Predict function cannot give me yearly estimates of psi. So, I`m using smoothed and projected values. Nevertheless, I would like to obtain estimates of psi along the elevation gradient for each year.
Is there a way to obtain these values in unmarked?

Thank you very much!

Best,

Marconi Campos

Marconi,

From my understanding (more knowledgeable folks should feel free to correct me), you need to predict initial psi and colonization (col) and extinction (ext) rates for each subsequent year, then project forward using this formula (using underscore for subscripts):

psi_t = (psi_t-1 x (1 - ext_t-1)) + (col_t-1 x (1 - psi_t-1))

In other words, psi in a year is calculated by psi in the previous year x those sites that don't go extinct (1-ext) plus the colonization rate for those sites that weren't occupied (1-psi).

I exported my prediction outputs to excel and set up stepwise calculations in a spreadsheet, but someone better at R should easily be able to do this in R with predict outputs.

You can predict with two covariates as below, depending on whether you are using year as a factor or continuous variable.

#One factor covar and one continuous covar.  Results will be predicted for each factor level when at mean continuous covar level.
NewData <- data.frame(Area=0, Observer=factor(c("AW","KE","NNC","Multiple","Other")))
Results.predict<-predict(fm, newdata=NewData,"det")
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#One factor covar and one continuous covar for psi.  Results will be predicted psi for continuous covar values for given factor level.
NewData <- data.frame(Area=seq(-0.8,5,by=0.1), Observer=factor("KE", levels=c("AW","KE","NNC","Multiple","Other")))
Results.predict<-predict(fm, "psi", newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#Two continuous covars (for interaction).  Must have same number of intervals, so use length.out instead of by interval
NewData <- data.frame(RRdist=seq(-1.2,3.2,length.out=20), ProporHab=seq(-3.3,1.1,length.out=20))
Results.predict <- predict(fm,"psi",newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#Two continuous covars (for interaction).  Mean of first covar and range of values for second
NewData <- data.frame(RRdist=0, ProporHab=seq(-3.3,1.1,by=0.1))
Results.predict <- predict(fm,"psi",newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

You can also use the min and max functions to population the sequence arguments in creating a data frame to predict into:
Instead of RRdist=seq(-1.2,3.2,length.out=20) use RRdist=seq(min(umf@siteCovs$RRdist, na.rm = TRUE),max(umf@siteCovs$RRdist, na.rm = TRUE),length.out=20)

Let me know if you have follow up questions.

-Alex

parts:
Please ignore if this is stating the obvious.  To "compare the elevation profile among the three years" you'll need to construct (explicitly) the associated "elevation profile" effect using the parameters in your model.  You'll then need to estimate the precision of that effect either using the Delta Method using the estimated covariance matrix from the colext output or  using a bootstrap.  Comparing the elevation profile among the three years is certainly a legitimate objective.  It just needs to be made explicit in terms of the parameters in the model.  That's the hard part.  Estimating the precision will be the easy (or at least easier) part.  I say all of this without a specific example because I don't see where you've given the model you're using.  (I'm reluctant to guess at the model just from the data frame you've presented.)

Jim

psi_t = (psi_t-1 x (1 - ext_t-1)) + (col_t-1 x (1 - psi_t-1))

#One factor covar and one continuous covar.  Results will be predicted for each factor level when at mean continuous covar level.
NewData <- data.frame(Area=0, Observer=factor(c("AW","KE","NNC","Multiple","Other")))

write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

Marconi,

From my understanding (more knowledgeable folks should feel free to correct me), you need to predict initial psi and colonization (col) and extinction (ext) rates for each subsequent year, then project forward using this formula (using underscore for subscripts):

psi_t = (psi_t-1 x (1 - ext_t-1)) + (col_t-1 x (1 - psi_t-1))

In other words, psi in a year is calculated by psi in the previous year x those sites that don't go extinct (1-ext) plus the colonization rate for those sites that weren't occupied (1-psi).

I exported my prediction outputs to excel and set up stepwise calculations in a spreadsheet, but someone better at R should easily be able to do this in R with predict outputs.

You can predict with two covariates as below, depending on whether you are using year as a factor or continuous variable.

#One factor covar and one continuous covar.  Results will be predicted for each factor level when at mean continuous covar level.
NewData <- data.frame(Area=0, Observer=factor(c("AW","KE","NNC","Multiple","Other")))
Results.predict<-predict(fm, newdata=NewData,"det")
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#One factor covar and one continuous covar for psi.  Results will be predicted psi for continuous covar values for given factor level.
NewData <- data.frame(Area=seq(-0.8,5,by=0.1), Observer=factor("KE", levels=c("AW","KE","NNC","Multiple","Other")))
Results.predict<-predict(fm, "psi", newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#Two continuous covars (for interaction).  Must have same number of intervals, so use length.out instead of by interval
NewData <- data.frame(RRdist=seq(-1.2,3.2,length.out=20), ProporHab=seq(-3.3,1.1,length.out=20))
Results.predict <- predict(fm,"psi",newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#Two continuous covars (for interaction).  Mean of first covar and range of values for second
NewData <- data.frame(RRdist=0, ProporHab=seq(-3.3,1.1,by=0.1))
Results.predict <- predict(fm,"psi",newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

You can also use the min and max functions to population the sequence arguments in creating a data frame to predict into:
Instead of RRdist=seq(-1.2,3.2,length.out=20) use RRdist=seq(min(umf@siteCovs$RRdist, na.rm = TRUE),max(umf@siteCovs$RRdist, na.rm = TRUE),length.out=20)

Marconi,

From my understanding (more knowledgeable folks should feel free to correct me), you need to predict initial psi and colonization (col) and extinction (ext) rates for each subsequent year, then project forward using this formula (using underscore for subscripts):

psi_t = (psi_t-1 x (1 - ext_t-1)) + (col_t-1 x (1 - psi_t-1))

In other words, psi in a year is calculated by psi in the previous year x those sites that don't go extinct (1-ext) plus the colonization rate for those sites that weren't occupied (1-psi).

I exported my prediction outputs to excel and set up stepwise calculations in a spreadsheet, but someone better at R should easily be able to do this in R with predict outputs.

You can predict with two covariates as below, depending on whether you are using year as a factor or continuous variable.

#One factor covar and one continuous covar.  Results will be predicted for each factor level when at mean continuous covar level.
NewData <- data.frame(Area=0, Observer=factor(c("AW","KE","NNC","Multiple","Other")))
Results.predict<-predict(fm, newdata=NewData,"det")
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#One factor covar and one continuous covar for psi.  Results will be predicted psi for continuous covar values for given factor level.
NewData <- data.frame(Area=seq(-0.8,5,by=0.1), Observer=factor("KE", levels=c("AW","KE","NNC","Multiple","Other")))
Results.predict<-predict(fm, "psi", newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#Two continuous covars (for interaction).  Must have same number of intervals, so use length.out instead of by interval
NewData <- data.frame(RRdist=seq(-1.2,3.2,length.out=20), ProporHab=seq(-3.3,1.1,length.out=20))
Results.predict <- predict(fm,"psi",newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#Two continuous covars (for interaction).  Mean of first covar and range of values for second
NewData <- data.frame(RRdist=0, ProporHab=seq(-3.3,1.1,by=0.1))
Results.predict <- predict(fm,"psi",newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

You can also use the min and max functions to population the sequence arguments in creating a data frame to predict into:
Instead of RRdist=seq(-1.2,3.2,length.out=20) use RRdist=seq(min(umf@siteCovs$RRdist, na.rm = TRUE),max(umf@siteCovs$RRdist, na.rm = TRUE),length.out=20)

Let me know if you have follow up questions.
